en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Nissaggiya Section (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Fifth Chapter on Pairs:
The Training Rule on Having Another Exchange for One’s Own.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was ill.
Then a certain lay follower approached the bhikkhunī Thullanandā; having approached, he said this to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā:
"I hope you are bearing up, noble lady; I hope you are getting by?"
“I am not well, friend; I cannot maintain myself.
“Noble lady, I will deposit a kahāpaṇa coin in the house of such-and-such a shopkeeper; from there, you may have whatever you wish brought to you.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā then instructed a certain female trainee: [to do so].
“Go, trainee nun, and bring a measure of oil for one kahāpaṇa from the house of such-and-such a shopkeeper.
Then that trainee nun, having brought a measure of oil for one kahāpaṇa from that shopkeeper’s house, gave it to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā spoke thus:
“I have no need for oil, trainee nun; I have need of ghee.
Then that trainee nun went to where the shopkeeper was; having approached him, she said this to the shopkeeper:
“It seems, friend, that the noble lady has no need for oil, but needs ghee. Here, take the oil and give me the ghee.”
“Venerable lady, if we were to take back goods that have already been sold, when would our goods ever be sold?
Oil has been taken away by the purchase of oil; bring the purchase-price for the ghee, and you shall take the ghee.
Then that trainee nun stood there weeping.
The bhikkhunīs said to that female trainee:
“Female trainee, why are you weeping?
Then that female trainee explained the matter to the bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the noble lady Thullanandā, having exchanged one thing, exchange for another? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having exchanged one thing, exchanges for another?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:

“… How can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having had one thing bartered for, have another thing bartered for? Bhikkhus, this is not fitting…” [as before] … “How can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having had one thing bartered for, have another thing bartered for?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [as before] … And thus,
monks, should the nuns recite this training rule:
‘If any nun, having requested one thing, should request another, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).’”
"But whichever" means whichever such... "nun" means...
[as before]... nun.
...pe... this is the nun intended in this context.
"Having had something else exchanged" means having exchanged anything whatsoever.
"Should she cause another to be bartered for" means: setting that aside, if she causes something else to be bartered for, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act;
with the acquisition [of the object], it becomes an offense involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It should be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to a single bhikkhunī.
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
…pe…
“Venerable ladies, this which I have caused to be exchanged for something else is an article to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
… “Let her give it” … “Let them give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the noble lady.
If she exchanges one thing for another while perceiving it as something else, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she exchanges one thing for another while being in doubt, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If it is another person, but she perceives them as not another, and she causes [an item] to be bartered for that other person, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If it is not another person, but she perceives them as another, and she causes [an item] to be bartered for that non-another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not another person, but she is in doubt, and she causes [an item] to be bartered for that non-another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one perceives what is not another as not another.
There is no offense if one exchanges that very thing and exchanges something else.
If she causes it to be procured after pointing out the benefit,
except for one who is insane or the first offender.
The fifth training rule is concluded.
